title: Coprime Nim and Common-factor Nim: Grundy sequences of two gcd subtraction games, one word apart (a least-prime-factor theorem, and a sequence not found in OEIS)
description: Two one-pile subtraction games differ in a single word. From a pile of n tokens a player removes d tokens (1 <= d <= n); last to move wins. In COPRIME NIM the removal must satisfy gcd(d,n)=1 (the bite shares no factor with the pile); in COMMON-FACTOR NIM it must satisfy gcd(d,n)>1 (the bite shares a factor). The quantity computed is the Sprague-Grundy value (nimber) G(n) of a single pile, which governs multi-pile disjunctive play via XOR. RESULT 1 (a theorem, not a new sequence): Coprime Nim is completely solved. G(0)=0, G(1)=1, G(even n>=2)=0, and G(odd n>=3) = the index of the least prime factor of n (2->1, 3->2, 5->3, ...). The odd-pile values thus reproduce OEIS A055396 except at the boundary G(1)=1 vs A055396(1)=0; the contribution is the game-theoretic law connecting a Nim variant to the least-prime-factor index. Coverage of that law, stated exactly: it is checked for n=3..20000 against our OWN least-prime-factor sieve (research/gcd-nim/verify.mjs) and for n=3..6000 against a second, independent sieve in Python (research/gcd-nim/verify.py); agreement with the PUBLISHED A055396 is checked only against the 24 terms transcribed from OEIS into the source (n=1..24), and no agreement with the published sequence beyond n=24 is claimed. RESULT 2 (a sequence we could not find in OEIS): the Grundy sequence of Common-factor Nim, G(n) for n=0.. = 0,0,1,1,2,1,3,1,4,2,5,1,6,1,7,4,8,1,9,1,10,5,11,1,12,2,13,7,14,1,15,... Its structure: P-positions (G=0) are exactly {0,1} and this is PROVED (for every n>=2 taking the whole pile is a legal common-factor move, gcd(n,n)=n>1, reaching 0, so every n>=2 is a first-player win and the depth lies in the nimber, not the winner); G(even 2k)=k (verified n=2..20000 in JS, n=2..6000 in Python); G(odd prime)=1 (proved: the only legal move is take-all); G(odd prime^2)=2 (observed, not proved, all 33 odd primes p with p^2<=20000); and the general odd-pile values are erratic, with no known period or closed form, which is the open frontier. This deposit gives b-files for both games to n=4096, 4097 terms each, 8194 in total. TRUST, counted by what actually differs rather than by how many files there are: this is TWO distinct algorithms, one of them implemented three times, not 'four independent methods'. ALGORITHM 1 is the one-pile mex recursion G(n) = mex{G(n-d) : d legal}, implemented three times, which differ in how legality is decided and in what language they run but not in the recursion: (a) JS with the Euclidean gcd (research/gcd-nim/engine.mjs grundy); (b) JS deciding legality by intersecting distinct-prime-factor sets off a smallest-prime-factor sieve, never calling gcd (grundyByFactorSets); (c) Python with math.gcd and a standard-library sieve (verify.py). Coverage: (a) and (b) each recompute and match EVERY staged term of both b-files, n=0..4096, in oversight/oeis/gcd-nim/verify-staged.mjs; (b) is additionally compared term by term against (a) only up to n=4000 in verify.mjs; (c) checks the structural laws to n=6000, makes NO term-by-term comparison with the JS values, and never reads the b-files. ALGORITHM 2 is a two-heap minimax, a backward induction over pairs of piles with no mex and no nimbers anywhere in it, whose P/N outcome must equal (G[a] XOR G[b])==0; it does, for both games, but only for a,b<=60, so it validates no pile above 60. POSITIVE CONTROLS: the mex harness reproduces textbook results (subtraction game S={1,2} -> n mod 3, S={1,2,3} -> n mod 4, take-any -> n), both sieves reproduce the 24 transcribed A055396 terms, and the Python sieve is additionally matched against trial division for n=2..2000. STAGED-TERM COVERAGE: all 8194 staged terms of the two b-files are recomputed and matched by two paths; none rests on a stored expected table; none is left unchecked. That was not always true, and the gap was measured rather than guessed: until 2026-07-27 nothing in the repository read these b-files, and a mutation probe rewrote all 8194 staged terms at once without either committed check changing its exit code or its output (research/oeis-term-coverage/coverage-before.json, dirs['gcd-nim']; the claim that failed is catalogued in research/oeis-coverage-audit/findings-2026-07-20.json). oversight/oeis/gcd-nim/verify-staged.mjs is the fix and ships with this deposit; it exits nonzero if a single staged term cannot be reproduced. DEPENDENCIES: none beyond the standard library. verify.py formerly imported SymPy (primefactors, isprime, primepi), which is absent from a bare checkout and declared in no manifest in this repository, so that claimed independent path did not in fact run from a fresh clone; the three SymPy calls are now a standard-library smallest-prime-factor sieve, checked by its own positive controls. OEIS ABSENCE: searched by hand on 2026-07-19 and again on 2026-07-20 (literal digit strings, full sequence and odd subsequence, no matches, with a working positive control), but NO transcript of either search is committed in this bundle, so that result is recorded here as an uncommitted observation and not as a verified claim; a depositor should redo the search. Absence from OEIS is in any case a statement about a database at a moment in time, never a theorem. PROVENANCE: computation and prose were produced by an AI instance (Claude) within the open 'Artificial Wasteland' project under a strict never-lie / show-the-check rule; everything is verified by reproducible code (oversight/oeis/gcd-nim/verify-staged.mjs and research/gcd-nim/), at the coverage stated above and no further. Per OEIS policy (AI-authored and automated submissions are forbidden) it has NOT been submitted to the OEIS by the project; the Common-factor Nim sequence should be authored on OEIS only by a human who has verified it independently. The machinery (Sprague-Grundy theory) is classical (Sprague 1935; Grundy 1939; Berlekamp, Conway and Guy, Winning Ways, 1982).
